We briefly establish some notation. Let P P be a distribution on a measurable space 𝒳 \mathcal{X} with density p p with respect to some reference measure μ \mu . If X X is a random variable with distribution P P , we write X ∼ P X\sim P . For a function f : 𝒳 → ℝ f:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} , we denote by 𝔼 P ​ [ f ​ ( X ) ] \mathbb{E}_{P}[f(X)] the expectation of f ⁡ ( X ) f(X) with respect to the distribution P P , that is, 𝔼 P ​ [ f ⁡ ( X ) ] = ∫ 𝒳 p ⁡ ( x ) ​ f ​ ( x ) ​ μ ​ ( 𝑑 x ) \mathbb{E}_{P}[f(X)]=\int_{\mathcal{X}}p(x)f(x)\,\mu(dx) . If Q Q is another distribution over 𝒳 \mathcal{X} , and Q Q has density q q with respect to μ \mu , the Kullback-Leibler divergence of P P from Q Q is
KL ( P ∥ Q ) = ∫ 𝒳 p ( x ) log ( p ⁡ ( x ) q ⁡ ( x ) ) μ ( d x ) . \textnormal{KL}(P\;\|\;Q)=\int_{\mathcal{X}}p(x)\log\Bigg(\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\Bigg)\,\mu(dx).

To simplify notation, we will denote a distribution by its density function. For instance, an expression of the form X ∼ p ⁡ ( X | Y ) X\sim p(X|Y) denotes that the random variable X X is distributed according to the conditional distribution of X X given Y Y .
3.1 Problem Statement

Consider a semi-supervised node classification problem, in which we have a graph dataset G = ( V , E ) G=(V,E) together with a node feature matrix X X , a collection of observed node labels, y y , and a collection of unobserved node labels y ∗ y^{*} , all of which are random samples. Motivated by the expressive power of the sheaf diffusion process, we model the conditional probability p θ ​ ( y | X ) p_{\theta}(y|X) using a sheaf neural network whose layers are given by Eq. 5 , with network parameters θ \theta and a cellular sheaf ℱ \mathcal{F} .

Rather than take the learned cellular sheaf ℱ \mathcal{F} (or sheaves) to be a deterministic function of X X as in [ 6 ] , we instead regard ℱ \mathcal{F} as a latent random variable of our model. See Figure 1 for a depiction of the probability graphical model. Note that the posterior distribution p θ ​ ( ℱ | X , y ) p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}|X,y) will be intractable due to the fact that the labels y y are modeled as the output of a neural network. Hence, to do approximate posterior inference of ℱ \mathcal{F} given the feature matrix, X X , the observed node labels y y , and model parameters θ \theta , we assume the intractable posterior distribution p θ ​ ( ℱ | X , y ) p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}|X,y) belongs to a predetermined family of variational distributions q ϕ ​ ( ℱ | X , y ) q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y) parameterized by weights ϕ \phi .
We begin by noting that the log-likelihood log ⁡ p θ ​ ( X , y ) \log p_{\theta}(X,y) can be written

log p θ ( X , y ) = KL ( q ϕ ( ℱ | X , y ) ∥ p θ ( ℱ | X , y ) ) + ℒ ( θ , ϕ ; X , y ) , \log p_{\theta}(X,y)=\textnormal{KL}(q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)\;\|\;p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}|X,y))+\mathcal{L}(\theta,\phi;X,y), (6)
where

ℒ ⁡ ( θ , ϕ , X , y ) := 𝔼 q ϕ ​ ( ℱ | X , y ) ​ [ − log ⁡ q ϕ ​ ( ℱ | X , y ) + log ⁡ p θ ​ ( ℱ , X , y ) ] . \mathcal{L}(\theta,\phi;X,y):=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)}\big[-\log q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)+\log p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F},X,y)\big]. (7)

The quantity ℒ ⁡ ( θ , ϕ , X , y ) \mathcal{L}(\theta,\phi;X,y) is known as the evidence lower bound or ELBO, due to the fact that the KL divergence from one distribution to another is always non-negative, hence log ⁡ p θ ​ ( X , y ) ≥ ℒ ⁡ ( θ , ϕ , X , y ) \log p_{\theta}(X,y)\geq\mathcal{L}(\theta,\phi,X,y) . Note from Eq. ( 6 ) that maximizing the ELBO with respect to the parameters θ \theta and ϕ \phi has the effect of maximizing the log-likelihood of the data, as well as minimizing the KL divergence of the variational distribution q ϕ ​ ( ℱ | X , y ) q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y) from the true posterior distribution p θ ​ ( ℱ | X , y ) p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}|X,y) . For this reason, the ELBO is commonly used as quantity to be optimized within variational Bayesian inference. See [ 5 ] for an overview of variational inference. In order to maximize ℒ ⁡ ( θ , ϕ , X , y ) \mathcal{L}(\theta,\phi;X,y) with respect to the parameters θ , ϕ \theta,\phi , we use the following equivalent expression:

ℒ ( θ , ϕ ; X , y ) = 𝔼 q ϕ ​ ( ℱ | X , y ) [ log p θ ( X , y | ℱ ) ] − KL ( q ϕ ( ℱ | X , y ) ∥ p θ ( ℱ ) ) . \mathcal{L}(\theta,\phi;X,y)=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)}\big[\log p_{\theta}(X,y|\mathcal{F})\big]-\textnormal{KL}(q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)\;\|\;p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F})). (8)

3.2 Variational Sheaf Learner

We consider a variational sheaf learner in three different cases: where the learned sheaf ℱ \mathcal{F} has restriction maps which are assumed to be (1) general linear, (2) special orthogonal, or (3) invertible diagonal. In all cases, we make the simplifying assumption that the variational distribution q ϕ ​ ( ℱ | X , y ) q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y) from the previous section factors as the product ∏ u ​ ⊴ ​ e q ϕ ​ ( ℱ u ​ ⊴ ​ e | X , y ) \prod_{u\trianglelefteq e}q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}|X,y) over all incident node-edge pairs u ​ ⊴ ​ e u\trianglelefteq e . While this assumption somewhat restricts the family of variational distributions, it makes computing the KL divergence term in the ELBO tractable. For further details, see Appendix C . We take each factor q ϕ ​ ( ℱ u ​ ⊴ ​ e | X , y ) q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}|X,y) to be a distribution Q ⁡ ( μ u ​ ⊴ ​ e , σ u ​ ⊴ ​ e ) Q(\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e},\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e}) which depends on the type of restriction map used within the sheaf, where the distributional parameters μ u ​ ⊴ ​ e , σ u ​ ⊴ ​ e \mu_{u\trianglelefteq e},\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e} are a function of the node features X X and ϕ \phi as follows. For each incident node-edge pair u ​ ⊴ ​ e u\trianglelefteq e , if u ′ ​ ⊴ ​ e u^{\prime}\trianglelefteq e denotes the other node incident with e e , a multi-layer perceptron with learned weights ϕ \phi , denoted MLP ϕ \MLP_{\phi} , maps the concatenated vector [ x u | | x u ′ ] [x_{u}||x_{u^{\prime}}] to distributional parameters μ u ​ ⊴ ​ e \mu_{u\trianglelefteq e} and σ u ​ ⊴ ​ e \sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e} :
[ μ u ​ ⊴ ​ e | | σ u ​ ⊴ ​ e ] = MLP ϕ ( [ x u | | x u ′ ] ) . [\,\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e}\,||\,\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e}\,]=\MLP_{\phi}([x_{u}||x_{u^{\prime}}]). (11)

Recall that a multi-layer perceptron is the composition of several feed-forward layers, each of which is a function of the form x ↦ σ ⁡ ( W ​ x + b ) x\mapsto\sigma(Wx+b) , where σ \sigma is a nonlinear activation function, in our case the exponential linear unit (ELU) [ 16 ] , W W is a weight matrix, and b b is a vector of biases.

Case 1: General Linear. In the case where the sheaf restriction maps ℱ u ​ ⊴ ​ e : ℱ ⁡ ( u ) → ℱ ⁡ ( e ) \mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}:\mathcal{F}(u)\to\mathcal{F}(e) are general linear maps, μ u ​ ⊴ ​ e \mu_{u\trianglelefteq e} and σ u ​ ⊴ ​ e \sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e} are d 2 d^{2} − - dimensional vectors. We take Q ⁡ ( μ u ​ ⊴ ​ e , σ u ​ ⊴ ​ e ) Q(\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e},\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e}) to be normal with diagonal covariance so that for z ∼ 𝒩 d 2 ​ ( μ u ​ ⊴ ​ e , diag ⁡ ( σ u ​ ⊴ ​ e ) ) z\sim\mathcal{N}_{d^{2}}(\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e},\diag(\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e})) we set ℱ u ​ ⊴ ​ e \mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e} to be the vector z z rearranged into a d × d d\times d matrix. The reparameterization trick in this case writes z = μ u ​ ⊴ ​ e + diag ⁡ ( σ u ​ ⊴ ​ e ) ​ ϵ z=\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e}+\diag(\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e})\epsilon for ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , I d 2 ) \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},I_{d^{2}}) so that ℱ u ​ ⊴ ​ e \mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e} , being the matrix obtained by reshaping the vector z z , is a deterministic function of μ u ​ ⊴ ​ e \mu_{u\trianglelefteq e} , σ u ​ ⊴ ​ e \sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e} , and ϵ \epsilon . We use a standard normal prior, where p θ ​ ( ℱ ) = ∏ u ​ ⊴ ​ e p θ ​ ( ℱ u ​ ⊴ ​ e ) p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F})=\prod_{u\trianglelefteq e}p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}) and p θ ​ ( ℱ u ​ ⊴ ​ e ) = 𝒩 d 2 ​ ( 𝟎 , I d 2 ) p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e})=\mathcal{N}_{d^{2}}(\mathbf{0},I_{d^{2}}) .

Case 2: Special Orthogonal. The case where sheaf restriction maps are assumed to be special orthogonal presents challenges. Typical probability distribution on S ​ O ​ ( d ) SO(d) , such as the matrix Langevin distribution, are not easily reparameterizable. This makes incorporating such distributions into neural networks, that are trained via back-propagation, difficult. On the other hand, while reparameterizable distributions on S ​ O ​ ( d ) SO(d) have been constructed in [ 21 ] using the exponential map, the density functions of such distributions can be difficult to compute exactly, which obstructs one from computing, or even efficiently estimating, the KL divergence term in Eq. ( 8 ). In Section 4 we define what we refer to as Cayley distributions, a family of reparameterizable distributions 𝒞 d ​ ( M , κ ) \mathcal{C}_{d}(M,\kappa) on S ​ O ​ ( d ) SO(d) with closed form expressions for their probability density functions. We use 𝒞 d ​ ( M , κ ) \mathcal{C}_{d}(M,\kappa) as the variational distributions for sheaves with special orthogonal restriction maps. Hence when ℱ u ​ ⊴ ​ e ∈ S ​ O ​ ( d ) \mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}\in SO(d) , the distributional parameters are a mean rotation μ u ​ ⊴ ​ e ∈ S ​ O ​ ( d ) \mu_{u\trianglelefteq e}\in SO(d) and scalar concentration parameter σ u ​ ⊴ ​ e ∈ [ 0 , 1 ) \sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e}\in[0,1) , and we have Q ⁡ ( μ u ​ ⊴ ​ e , σ u ​ ⊴ ​ e ) = 𝒞 d ​ ( μ u ​ ⊴ ​ e , σ u ​ ⊴ ​ e ) Q(\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e},\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e})=\mathcal{C}_{d}(\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e},\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e}) . The reparameterization of the Cayley distributions is described in Remark 4.3 . We use a prior distribution p θ ​ ( ℱ ) = ∏ u ​ ⊴ ​ e p θ ​ ( ℱ u ​ ⊴ ​ e ) p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F})=\prod_{u\trianglelefteq e}p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}) where each p θ ​ ( ℱ u ​ ⊴ ​ e ) p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}) is a uniform distribution on S ​ O ​ ( d ) SO(d) .

Case 3: Invertible Diagonal. In the case where the sheaf restriction maps ℱ u ​ ⊴ ​ e : ℱ ⁡ ( u ) → ℱ ⁡ ( e ) \mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}:\mathcal{F}(u)\to\mathcal{F}(e) are assumed to be invertible diagonal matrices with respect to the standard basis, μ u ​ ⊴ ​ e \mu_{u\trianglelefteq e} and σ u ​ ⊴ ​ e \sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e} are d d − - dimensional vectors and we take q ϕ ​ ( ℱ u ​ ⊴ ​ e | X , y ) = Q ⁡ ( μ u ​ ⊴ ​ e , σ u ​ ⊴ ​ e ) q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}|X,y)=Q(\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e},\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e}) to be a normal distribution with diagonal covariance, so that ℱ u ​ ⊴ ​ e = diag ⁡ ( z ) \mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}=\diag(z) for z ∼ 𝒩 d ​ ( μ u ​ ⊴ ​ e , diag ⁡ ( σ u ​ ⊴ ​ e ) ) z\sim\mathcal{N}_{d}(\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e},\diag(\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e})) . The reparameterization ℱ = g ϕ ​ ( X , ϵ ) \mathcal{F}=g_{\phi}(X,\epsilon) in this case is given by setting ℱ u ​ ⊴ ​ e = diag ⁡ ( μ u ​ ⊴ ​ e + σ u ​ ⊴ ​ e ​ ϵ ) \mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}=\diag(\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e}+\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e}\epsilon) for ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , I d ) \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},I_{d}) . Lastly, we use a standard normal prior, where p θ ​ ( ℱ ) = ∏ u ​ ⊴ ​ e p θ ​ ( ℱ u ​ ⊴ ​ e ) p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F})=\prod_{u\trianglelefteq e}p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}) and p θ ​ ( ℱ u ​ ⊴ ​ e ) = 𝒩 d ​ ( 𝟎 , I d ) p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e})=\mathcal{N}_{d}(\mathbf{0},I_{d}) .

We give an overview of the Bayesian sheaf neural network architecture, which is also summarized in 2 . The variational sheaf learning mechanism maps the input node features to the sheaf distributional parameters as described in Section 3.2 , though we briefly describe here as well. A linear layer first resizes the input node features to dimension k k . Specifically, we use k = d ​ f k=df where d d and f f are the stalk dimensions and number of feature channels respectively. Then, for each incident node-edge pair u ​ ⊴ ​ e u\trianglelefteq e , the features of the pair of nodes corresponding to the edge e e are concatenated. Hence a node feature matrix of size n × k n\times k is transformed by this concatenation operation into a matrix of size 2 ​ e × 2 ​ k 2e\times 2k , where n n denotes the number of nodes, and e e denotes the number of edges in the graph. Lastly, an MLP maps these features indexed by the incident node-edge pairs u ​ ⊴ ​ e u\trianglelefteq e to distributional parameters μ u ​ ⊴ ​ e \mu_{u\trianglelefteq e} and σ u ​ ⊴ ​ e \sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e} as described by Eq. ( 11 ), which define the distribution over the cellular sheaves. From this distribution, a collection of independent and identically distributed sheaves ℱ 1 , ℱ 2 , … , ℱ L \mathcal{F}_{1},\mathcal{F}_{2},\dots,\mathcal{F}_{L} are sampled: one for each layer of the network.

Separately, a multi-layer perceptron maps the input node features X ∈ ℝ n × m X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m} to features of dimension X ′ ∈ ℝ n × d ​ f X^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times df} where d d is the stalk dimension and f f is the number of hidden channels. The features X ′ X^{\prime} are reshaped to size n ​ d × f nd\times f . Sheaf layers described by Eq. ( 5 ) update the transformed features X ′ X^{\prime} using the sampled sheaves ℱ 1 , ℱ 2 , … , ℱ L \mathcal{F}_{1},\mathcal{F}_{2},\dots,\mathcal{F}_{L} . Finally, a linear layer maps the output of the final sheaf layer to a vector of class probabilities.

During training, a one-sample Monte Carlo estimate of Eq. ( 9 ) or Eq. ( 10 ) is computed, and the loss is back-propagated to update the network weights. During testing, ensembling is performed to obtain point estimates for the unobserved node labels y ∗ y^{*} .
